title: Question 2

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that the number of gas molecules in the cylinder is $1.4 \times 10^{23}$.

markscheme_points.guidance: or pV = nRT and nNA = N

hints: Hint 1: Start by listing what you know for the gas in SI units - pressure $p$, volume $V$ and thermodynamic temperature $T$ in kelvin - and think about which gas law links these bulk properties to the total number of particles $N$.

Hint 2: Rearrange the molecular form of the ideal gas law to make $N$ the subject, then substitute $p = 3.3 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$, $V = 1.8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$, $T = 310 \text{ K}$ and $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J K}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link bulk properties to particle number**
For an ideal gas, pressure and temperature arise from the motion of a huge number of molecules. The link is $$pV = NkT$$ where $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J K}^{-1}$ is the Boltzmann constant and $N$ is the number of molecules.

Step 2: **Rearrange and substitute**
Make $N$ the subject: $$N = \frac{pV}{kT}$$ Then: $$N = \frac{(3.3 \times 10^5) \times (1.8 \times 10^{-3})}{(1.38 \times 10^{-23}) \times 310}$$ $$N = 1.39 \times 10^{23} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{23}$$ This confirms the given value. Remember $T$ must already be in kelvin.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Use kinetic theory to explain why, when the piston is moved so that the gas expands, this causes a decrease in the temperature of the gas.

markscheme_points.text: speed of molecule decreases on impact with moving piston
mean square speed (directly) proportional to (thermodynamic) temperature
markscheme_points.guidance: or mean square speed (directly) proportional to kinetic energy (of molecules) or kinetic energy (of molecules) (directly) proportional to (thermodynamic temperature)

markscheme_points.text: kinetic energy (of molecules) decreases (so temperature decreases)

hints: Hint 1: Picture a single molecule hitting the piston in Fig. 2.1 while the piston is moving outwards to the left - does the molecule rebound with the same speed as it had before, like hitting a fixed wall?
Hint 2: Think about what happens to the average kinetic energy of all the molecules if every collision with the receding piston leaves them a little slower.
Hint 3: Recall how absolute temperature is related in kinetic theory to mean molecular kinetic energy or to mean square speed, and use that to connect slower molecules to lower temperature.
parts.proper_answer: Molecules rebound with reduced speed from the receding piston, so mean square speed and mean kinetic energy decrease. Since mean kinetic energy is proportional to thermodynamic temperature, temperature falls.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Collisions with a moving wall**
With a fixed wall, an elastic collision reverses the normal component of velocity with no change in speed. Here the piston is moving away from the gas. Think of a tennis ball hitting a racket moving away - it comes off slower. So each molecule that hits the piston rebounds with a smaller speed than it had before impact.

Step 2: **From slower molecules to lower temperature**
Many such collisions reduce the average speed of the whole gas. In kinetic theory, thermodynamic temperature $T$ is a direct measure of average translational kinetic energy: $$\frac{1}{2}m<c^2> \propto kT$$ where $<c^2>$ is mean square speed. Less mean kinetic energy means smaller $<c^2>$ and therefore lower $T$. That is why expansion against a moving piston cools the gas.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The gas expands so that its volume increases to $2.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{m}^3$ at a pressure of $2.3 \times 10^5 \text{Pa}$ and a temperature of $288 \text{K}$, as shown in Fig. 2.2.

{{figure:figure_2_2}}
parts.text:
The average translational kinetic energy $E_{\text{K}}$ of a molecule of an ideal gas is given by

$$E_{\text{K}} = \frac{3}{2}kT$$

where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the thermodynamic temperature.

Calculate the increase in internal energy $\Delta U$ of the gas during the expansion.
hints: Hint 1: For an ideal gas there is no potential energy between molecules, so what does the total internal energy $U$ consist of, and how is it related to the average energy $E_K$ of one molecule and the number $N$?

Hint 2: Since $E_K = (3/2)kT$, the change depends only on the temperature change $\Delta T = 288 - 310 \text{ K}$ - work out the sign of $\Delta T$ first and think about whether $U$ should increase or decrease.
Hint 3: Multiply the change per molecule by $N = 1.4 \times 10^{23}$ to get $\Delta U = (3/2)Nk\Delta T$ and evaluate with $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J K}^{-1}$.
parts.proper_answer: $\Delta U = (3/2)Nk\Delta T = -64 \text{ J}$ (decrease of about $64 \text{ J}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Internal energy is total kinetic energy**
An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so internal energy $U$ is just the sum of the translational kinetic energies of all $N$ molecules: $$U = N E_K = N \times \frac{3}{2}kT$$ Therefore a change in temperature gives: $$\Delta U = \frac{3}{2}Nk\Delta T$$

Step 2: **Find the temperature change**
$$\Delta T = 288 - 310 = -22 \text{ K}$$ The negative sign already tells you internal energy will decrease.

Step 3: **Substitute numbers**
$$\Delta U = \frac{3}{2} \times (1.4 \times 10^{23}) \times (1.38 \times 10^{-23}) \times (-22)$$ $$\Delta U \approx -64 \text{ J}$$ So the increase is $-64 \text{ J}$, i.e. a decrease of $64 \text{ J}$.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text:
The work done by the gas during the expansion is $76 \text{J}$.

Use your answer in (i) to explain whether thermal energy is transferred to or from the gas during the expansion.

markscheme_points.text: decrease in internal energy is less than work done by gas
(thermal energy is) transferred to the gas (during the expansion)

hints: Hint 1: Compare the two energy numbers you now have - the gas loses about $64 \text{ J}$ of internal energy but it does $76 \text{ J}$ of work pushing the piston out - can the lost internal energy alone pay for that work?

Hint 2: Use energy conservation for the gas, $\Delta U = q + w_{on}$, or in words: change in internal energy = thermal energy supplied + work done on the gas. If work done by the gas exceeds the drop in $U$, what must be true about $q$?
parts.proper_answer: Work done by gas (76 J) is greater than decrease in internal energy (64 J), so extra energy must be supplied as heat. Thermal energy is transferred to the gas.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply energy conservation**
Doing work by expansion costs energy. The first law says: $$\Delta U = q + w_{on}$$ where $q$ is heat supplied to the gas and $w_{on}$ is work done on the gas. Here $w_{on} = -76 \text{ J}$ because work is done by the gas, and $\Delta U = -64 \text{ J}$ from (i).

Step 2: **Spot the shortfall**
The fall in internal energy, $64 \text{ J}$, is less than the $76 \text{ J}$ needed for the work. Rearranging: $$q = \Delta U - w_{on} = -64 - (-76) = +12 \text{ J}$$ Positive $q$ means net thermal energy flows into the gas from the surroundings during the expansion to make up the difference.
